<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{1}
Let $D\subset\Bbb R^n$ be a bounded strictly convex domain. Assume that $(D,d)$ is a proper
geodesic metric space, $d$ induces the Euclidean topology on $D$, and the $d$-balls are
convex in the Euclidean sense. Then $(D,d)$ is visible.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{2} Let $D\subset\Bbb C^N$ be a bounded domain which is locally strictly
convexifiable near any boundary point. Then $(D,k_D)$ is visible.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Fix $o\in D$ and set
$$(x|y)_o=\frac12\bigl(d(x,o)+d(y,o)-d(x,y)\bigr),\qquad x,y\in D.$$
Although \cite[Proposition~2.5]{BNT} is stated for $k_D$ ($D\subset\Bbb C^N)$, its proof uses
only compactness of closed bounded balls and the agreement of the metric and Euclidean
topologies. Therefore $(D,d)$ is visible if and only if for any two distinct points
$p,q\in\partial D,$
$$\limsup_{(x,y)\to(p,q)}(x|y)_o<\infty.$$

Suppose that $(D,d)$ is not visible. Then there exist two distinct points
$p,q\in\partial D$ and sequences $x_j\to p$, $y_j\to q$ such that
$(x_j|y_j)_o\to+\infty.$ Let $\sigma_j$ be a $d$-geodesic from $x_j$ to $y_j$.
Because $0\le d(o,x_j)-(x_j|y_j)_o\le d(x_j,y_j)$, we may choose $z_j\in\sigma_j$
so that $d(x_j,z_j)=d(o,x_j)-(x_j|y_j)_o.$ By boundedness of $D$, after passing to a subsequence,
$z_j\to r\in\overline D$. Since $d(o,z_j)\ge (x_j|y_j)_o\to+\infty$, the agreement of the two
topologies implies $r\in\partial D$. As $p\neq q$, we may assume that $p\neq r$. Since
$d(x_j,z_j)-d(x_j,o)=-(x_j|y_j)_o\to-\infty$ and the $d$-balls are convex,
\cite[Proposition~4.3]{HW} yields $[r,p]\subset\partial D$, a contradiction to the strict
convexity of $D$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Let $D\subset\Bbb C^N$ be a bounded strictly convex domain. By \cite[Theorem~3]{V}, 
all $k_D$-balls are strictly convex. A midpoint argument then shows that a real $k_D$-geodesic is 
uniquely determined by its endpoints. Consequently, the complex geodesic through any two distinct
points of $D$ is unique up to precomposition with an automorphism of the unit disc $\Bbb D$ (such 
geodesics exist by Lempert's theorem). Recall that a complex geodesic is a holomorphic isometric
embedding $\varphi:(\Bbb D,k_{\Bbb D})\rightarrow(D,k_D)$.

In this direction, note that combining Corollary \ref{2} with \cite[Proposition~4 and Corollary~6]{N} 
gives the following: every complex geodesic of $D$ extends continuously to $\overline{\Bbb D}$ and 
maps $\partial\Bbb D$ into $\partial D$; for any two distinct point $p,q\in\overline D$, there 
exists a complex geodesic $\varphi$ such that $p,q\in\varphi(\overline{\Bbb D})$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
